query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Creep resistance in the FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy protective coating is enhanced by inducing serrated grain boundaries during post-fabrication heat treatment. These serrated boundaries, achieved by controlled cooling that coarsens L12 precipitates, pin grain boundaries and redistribute local strains, thereby delaying intergranular void formation and crack propagation under sustained stress.
generation.material_initial_state: As-fabricated high-entropy alloy coating with a primarily FCC matrix containing uniformly dispersed L12 precipitates and straight (non-serrated) grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: A controlled solution heat treatment with a reduced cooling rate designed to promote precipitate coarsening and induce serrated grain boundary morphology.
generation.conditions: Continuous high-temperature loading (approximately 650°C) under constant stress conditions that simulate service conditions for protective coatings.
generation.structural_mediator: Serrated grain boundaries facilitated by the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates at the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The serrated grain boundaries redistribute and mitigate local strain concentration, reducing the susceptibility to intergranular void nucleation and crack propagation that typically lead to plastic deformation and creep failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline material with straight grain boundaries, the treated coating will exhibit significantly improved creep rupture life (potentially by an order of magnitude), lower steady-state creep rates, and more uniform strain distribution across grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy in its as-fabricated state with straight grain boundaries and no post-treatment modification.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under sustained high-temperature (around 650°C) and constant loading conditions; deviations from these conditions (e.g., much lower temperatures or cyclic loading) may not show the same degree of enhanced performance.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether this mechanism applies equally to high-entropy alloys with mixed FCC/BCC phase structures or under long-term operational environments that may induce additional microstructural changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy coatings: one set undergoes the controlled solution heat treatment to induce serrated grain boundaries, while the second set remains in the as-fabricated state with straight boundaries. Subject both sets to standardized creep tests at 650°C under a constant applied stress.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain boundary morphology and precipitate coarsening) using microscopy techniques such as SEM or TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., longer time-to-rupture, lower creep strain rate, or more uniform strain distribution) compared to the baseline specimens, or if similar performance enhancements are observed without the presence of serrated grain boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
